tagline.text: Right next to Boracay, an old Boracay where time seems to have stopped

children.text: A small island in Romblon just over
1 hour
by boat from Boracay, known locally as Hambil. With its less-developed white sand beaches, cliff-diving spots, and cave exploration, it's popular with travelers looking to escape Boracay's crowds.

Administratively, Carabao Island belongs to Romblon province, but geographically it's a small island right next to Caticlan at the northern tip of Panay and just north of Boracay. The whole island is a single municipality called San Jose, and locals call it 'Hambil' after its old name. It's close enough that on a clear day you can see the island's ridgeline over the horizon from Boracay's Station 1 beach.

What draws attention to this island is an atmosphere that recalls 'Boracay 20 to 30 years ago.' It has fine white sand similar to Boracay's, but no large resorts, malls, or all-night parties. Most islanders work in fishing and farming; bangkas line the beach, and in the evening children swim in the sea. With fewer tourist facilities there are inconveniences too, but that simplicity is exactly the appeal.

The terrain is characterized by limestone cliffs, so caves and rock ledges are common along the coast. This has made Carabao Island known as a cliff-diving spot in the western Visayas, and you can also swim into sea caves. The beaches on the island's west and south sides are good spots to see the sunset together with a view of Boracay.

It suits travelers who want to rest somewhere quiet for a day or two during a Boracay trip, young travelers who love adventurous water play, and those who want a close look at everyday life in a Philippine island village. On the other hand, travelers who want convenient facilities and a variety of restaurants would be better off with just a day trip.

The island's most famous cliff-diving spot, with rock ledges of varying heights to jump from into the sea. It also has an underwater cave passage, making it popular with confident swimmers, and the entrance fee is about
A coastal cave with an interior space as tall as a cathedral ceiling, with a diving platform set up inside for jumping into the sea. It's safer to enter with a local guide.
The long white sand beach on the island's southwest side has fine sand and clear water, often compared to Boracay's White Beach. With few crowds, it feels like you have the whole beach to yourself.
A viewpoint on a hilltop farm, a sunset spot with a view of Boracay Island across the water. The entrance fee is around
, and it's best to arrive
30 minutes
before sunset.

Hire a motorcycle taxi for half a day and tour the beaches, caves, and viewpoints all at once. The driver, who knows the island's road conditions and the locations of its sights, effectively acts as a guide.
A cave once home to countless bats, where you can see the island's limestone terrain up close. The interior is dark and slippery, so bring a flashlight and sturdy shoes.
Hire a bangka and go snorkeling around the island's coral areas and small beaches. With fewer boats than Boracay, many spots have relatively better coral condition.

From Manila to Caticlan Airport (MPH) takes about
1 hour
, and about
1 hour 5 minutes
to Kalibo Airport (KLO). Caticlan Airport is much more convenient since it's close to the port; if you land at Kalibo, you'll need another
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by van to Caticlan. There are also direct flights to Caticlan and Kalibo from Cebu.
Passenger bangkas to San Jose depart several times a day from Tabon Port in Caticlan or nearby jetties. Most leave around
8–9 AM
and
1–3 PM
, taking about
1–1.5 hours
depending on sea conditions, with fares around
per person. Passenger bangkas returning from the island to Caticlan mostly leave around
, with some also around
. Schedules change frequently depending on weather and boat operators, so be sure to check with your accommodation or the port the day before.
To go directly from Boracay, charter a bangka near Station 1. Depending on group size and negotiation, it's about
one way and takes about
40 minutes–1 hour
. Bangkas also run to and from the Romblon mainland and Tablas Island (Santa Fe), so you can connect it with a Romblon island trip.
The island has almost no taxis or jeepneys; habal-habal (motorcycle taxis) are the main mode of transport. A half-day to full-day charter to tour the sights is negotiated at around
per person. There are also a few tricycles.
The dry season from
November
to
May
is best. January to
April
especially has calm seas and clear skies, suited to bangka travel and cliff diving. March to
May
is very hot, but the water color is at its most beautiful.
From
June
to
October

is the rainy season, and the southwest monsoon roughens the sea on the island's west side. During this period, the small bangkas linking Caticlan and the island are often canceled, and the Philippine Coast Guard sometimes suspends small-boat operations. Typhoons mostly pass through this area from July to
November
, so build extra time into your schedule. Pairing your trip with nearby Kalibo's Ati-Atihan Festival (the third week of
January
) also lets you enjoy Panay's festival atmosphere.

Accommodation is scattered around White Beach and Lanas Beach. Local guesthouses run about
a night, and beachfront bungalows and small resorts about
. There are a few mid-range resorts with pools, but since there are few of them, book ahead during peak season (December–
May
) and holidays. Most accommodations either serve meals or let you use a kitchen.

There aren't many restaurants on the island, so most travelers rely on their accommodation's restaurant and local carinderias (small eateries). Grilled fish caught that day, squid, shellfish dishes, and kinilaw are common, and in the morning you can buy fresh fish at the market near the port and ask your accommodation to cook it. There are no convenience stores or large supermarkets, so buy snacks, bottled water, and your favorite drinks in Caticlan beforehand.
There are no ATMs on the island. Withdraw enough cash in Caticlan or Boracay to cover accommodation, transport, and entrance fees.
Mobile signal is generally available, but weak in the island's interior and near the caves. Accommodation Wi-Fi can also be slow.
Public boats leaving the island often depart at dawn, so it's safer to be back in Caticlan or Boracay the day before your return flight.
Before cliff diving, always check the water depth and safe entry points with a local guide, and start from the lower spots first.
Aqua shoes and a waterproof bag are essential. The caves and rocky shoreline are slippery and sharp.
Before boarding a habal-habal, clearly agree on the route, total fare, and waiting time.
In Caticlan, you need to go to the jetty where Carabao Island bangkas dock, not the jetty port for Boracay. Tell your tricycle driver clearly that you're headed 'to Hambil' or 'to San Jose.'
Cliff diving carries a high risk of injury. Never jump after drinking, and wear a life vest if you're not a confident swimmer.
Small bangkas rock heavily in high waves. Wear a life vest, and don't insist on departing when weather conditions are bad.
There's no large hospital on the island, so emergencies require transport to Caticlan or Kalibo. Be sure to bring a basic medical kit.
Don't leave trash on the beaches or in the caves, and don't damage the coral or cave life.
Roads are dark at night, so avoid riding a motorcycle late in the evening.
Boat services can be canceled without notice depending on the weather. Always build in about a day of buffer time for this island.
